big: Rohan tried three budgets in one year and quit each by March. The method was not the problem. The setup was. Let us look at what actually makes a budget stick.

lines: I cannot keep track of every rupee. Is there a simpler way?
Yes. Start with one rule, one habit and one trick. The rule splits your pay, the habit saves first and the trick handles yearly bills.

alt: A bar split into needs, wants and savings
caps: About half goes to needs: rent, food, bills, EMIs, insurance.
About 30% goes to wants: eating out, travel, shopping.
About 20% goes to savings and investing, taken out first.
A starting point, not a law. If rent is high, adjust the split and keep saving.

intro: A sinking fund spreads a yearly cost over twelve months.
note: Total divided by twelve. The big bills then arrive to money that is already waiting.

q: Rohan saves whatever is left at the end of the month. By month-end, little is left. What habit fixes this?
opts: Spend much less in the first week, so more remains for saving later on
Keep a note of the savings goal on the fridge as a daily reminder
Wait until the end of the month and decide how much to save then
Move savings out on salary day by standing instruction, before spending
why: Willpower in week one does not last. A rule that does not rely on mood works better.
A reminder depends on memory and effort, while an automatic transfer does not.
Deciding at month-end repeats the problem, since spending has already taken what is left.
Paying yourself first means the saving leaves on salary day and the rest is spent from what remains.

q: Meena earns ₹60,000 and her rent plus bills are already ₹38,000. How should she use the 50-30-20 rule?
opts: Drop the rule entirely, since it does not match her situation at all
Use it as a guide, shrink wants, and still protect her saving
Cut her saving to zero so that needs and wants both fit
Move to a cheaper house within a week, whatever it takes
why: The rule is a starting point. When it does not fit, adjust it rather than throw it away.
Needs above half mean wants must shrink, but saving should still come first, even if smaller.
Cutting saving to zero leaves nothing for emergencies or goals, so it should be the last cut.
A rushed move can add costs and stress. Adjusting the split is quicker and gentler.

q: A family's yearly costs are ₹72,000 across insurance, school fees and festivals. What does a sinking fund suggest?
opts: Keep the money in the main account and hope the bills do not clash
Pay each bill on its due date from whatever is left that month
Set aside ₹6,000 each month in a separate place for these bills
Borrow on a credit card when the bills arrive and repay slowly
why: Leaving it in the main account lets everyday spending eat into it, and the bills still arrive.
Paying from what is left is what makes big bills feel like shocks in the month they land.
Dividing ₹72,000 by twelve gives ₹6,000 a month, and the money is ready when each bill comes.
Card interest is high, so borrowing for expected bills is the costliest way to handle them.

opts: Every rupee is given a job, so income minus plans comes to zero
A budget that sets all spending to zero for the whole month ahead
A plan that only covers the single costs that are above ₹10,000 a month
A budget that starts afresh every year with no use of past data
why: Each rupee is assigned to a need, want, saving or debt before the month starts.
It does not mean zero spending. Zero is what is left unassigned after every rupee has a job.
It covers all income and spending, not only large items above a set amount.
The word zero refers to the unassigned balance, not to restarting the plan each year.

pts: Start with 50-30-20 as a guide, then adjust to your own costs.
Pay yourself first: move savings out on salary day.
Use a sinking fund so yearly bills do not wreck a month.
